prompt: Which statement is the INVERSE of "If a road is icy, then the bridge is closed"?

choices.label: If a road is not icy, then the bridge is not closed
If the bridge is not closed, then the road is not icy
If the bridge is closed, then the road is icy
If a road is icy, then the bridge is not closed

hint: Three relatives to keep straight: converse (swap), inverse (negate), contrapositive (swap AND negate).

hints.text: Three relatives to keep straight: converse (swap), inverse (negate), contrapositive (swap AND negate).

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Practice on a tiny sentence: for "If it rains, then I carry an umbrella," the inverse is "If it does NOT rain, then I do NOT carry an umbrella" — both parts negated, order unchanged. Make the same edit here.
The inverse negates both parts but keeps them in the SAME order.
Not icy ⇒ not closed, in the original order. That is choice A.

explanation: For "if $p$, then $q$," the inverse is "if not $p$, then not $q$" — both parts negated, order unchanged.
Negating "a road is icy" and "the bridge is closed" in place gives choice A.
Choice B is the contrapositive (swapped and negated), choice C is the converse (swapped only), and choice D negates just the conclusion, which is none of the three.

alternativeExplanations.title: Two questions, in order
steps: Question 1: did the parts trade places? For the inverse, no.
Question 2: did both parts get negated? For the inverse, yes. Only choice A answers no-then-yes.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The classic trap is choice B, the contrapositive — it also has two "nots," so it looks right at a glance.

Check the ORDER first, before you count the "nots." The original starts with the road; the inverse must also start with the road. Choice B starts with the bridge, so it is the contrapositive, not the inverse.
